instructions:
You are judging translations of one English original into Australian English vernacular. The candidates
are anonymous (A, B, C ...) and in random order; they may come from a rule engine, a language model or a
person. Judge each against the original and against the brief: the level of Aussie (1 tourist: a light
touch; 5 swaggie: a full pub yarn) and the vulgarity allowed (0 nan: no swearing; 1 dad: bloody, bugger,
bastard; 2 uncle-bob: piss, arse, fuck; 3 tradie: the c-word too). A candidate is neither better nor worse
for being longer, or for using more slang than the brief asks for.

Each criterion measures one thing, so one weakness costs a candidate once. How much Aussie there is, against
the brief, is register; how natural the Aussie that is there sounds is authenticity. A text left largely
untranslated scores low on register, and is judged on authenticity, tone and essence by what it does say.
The change of voice the brief asks for (a press release told as a yarn) is not a loss of tone. An aside that
reacts to or elaborates something in the original is colour; a new fact, event or claim is invented, and
counts against meaning.

For each candidate and each criterion, write the evidence first: what you saw, quoting the candidate
verbatim in double quotes. Then give the score. Use the anchors; a 2 or a 4 sits between them. Then list
the candidate's specific problems, each with a verbatim quote from the candidate, the original passage it
renders (empty when the line is added and renders nothing), a severity (critical: changes or loses meaning
that matters; major: wrong sense, wrong register, or something an Australian would wince at; minor: a
weaker choice), and why. A problem that runs through the whole text is listed once, with one
representative quote. Last, rank the candidates on each comparison criterion and overall: a list of tiers,
best first, each tier the candidates you can't separate (most tiers hold one).

CRITERIA
- meaning: Does it say everything the original says, and nothing that changes it?
    1: Events, facts or claims lost or changed; a reader would come away with a different story.
    3: The gist survives, but some details are lost, changed or invented.
    5: Every point survives; additions are colour that hangs off something in the original.
- sense: Does every Aussie term carry the original's sense in its context?
    1: Several terms took the wrong sense ("the latest version" as gossip, "terrible" as rude).
    3: One or two terms took the wrong sense, or strain to fit.
    5: Every term fits its context exactly.
- authenticity: Would an Australian hear the Aussie it uses as natural, not a tourist's pastiche (however much or little there is)?
    1: Stage-Australian; stock phrases bolted on; US or British forms left in.
    3: Mostly natural, with some stock or forced lines.
    5: Sounds like a real Australian talking; idiom used the way locals use it.
- register: Is it as Aussie, and as vulgar, as the brief asked, no more and no less?
    1: Far off the brief (a level-1 brief told as a pub yarn, or swearing past the vulgarity allowed).
    3: Somewhat off: noticeably heavier or lighter than asked.
    5: Exactly the weight the brief asked for.
- tone: Does it keep the original's tone under the slang (solemn stays solemn, a joke stays a joke)? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: The tone is lost or inverted (a eulogy played for laughs, a warning made flippant).
    3: The tone wobbles in places.
    5: The original's tone comes through whole.
- flow: Does it read smoothly aloud, without pile-ups, clunky joins or repetition? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: Hard to read; stacked synonyms, broken grammar, jarring joins.
    3: Readable, with some clunky stretches.
    5: Reads like it was written that way.
- variety: Does it vary its slang, openers and tags, rather than leaning on a few? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: The same few terms or tics over and over.
    3: Some repetition a reader would notice.
    5: Varied throughout, with nothing leaned on.
- essence: Leaving aside how much it is retold (that is register), does it keep what the original is about and what makes it itself, its point, shape and character? (also ranked across candidates)
    1: Could be a different text; what made the original distinctive is gone.
    3: Recognisably the original, but flattened.
    5: Unmistakably the original, retold.

ORIGINAL:
The following are the duties of this position at the GS-12. If you are selected at a lower grade level, you will have the opportunity to learn to perform all these duties, and will receive training to help you grow in this position.

As a TECHNICAL WRITER-EDITOR, you will:

Properly manipulate the contents of documents and of Federal Register publications to ensure legally effective, timely, and accurate publication of them.

Manage work, whether done independently, as a team member, or in leading others, to achieve timely, accurate publication of all documents and accomplish all program goals.

Understand and appropriately address customer needs associated with all aspects of the Federal Register publication process in fulfillment of the Office of the Federal Register's program responsibilities.

Understand and properly use the technical resources available for, and associated with the Federal Register publications processes, including information technology, legacy systems, and other technical resources.

Requirements

Conditions of employment

This opportunity is also open to Status Candidates under Announcement ST-12632063-25-SW.

Please refer to that announcement for details on open period, eligibility, and how to apply.

The experience may have been gained in either the public, private sector or volunteer service. One year of experience refers to full-time work; part-time work is considered on a prorated basis. To ensure full credit for your work experience, please indicate dates of employment by month/day/year, and indicate number of hours worked per week on your resume.

A one year probationary period may be required.

Must successfully complete a background investigation.

Complete a Declaration for Federal Employment to determine your suitability for Federal employment, at the time requested by the agency.

If you are a male applicant born after December 31, 1959, certify that you have registered with the Selective Service System or are exempt from having to do so.

Go through a Personal Identity Verification (PIV) process that requires two forms of identification from the Form i-9. Federal law requires verification of the identity and employment eligibility of all new hires in the U.S.

Please refer to "Conditions of Employment."

Click "Print Preview" to review the entire announcement before applying.

Must be U.S. Citizens or U.S. Nationals.

Qualifications

You must meet the following requirements by the closing date of this announcement.

Specialized Experience: For the GS-09, you must have one year of specialized experience at a level of difficulty and responsibility equivalent to the GS-07 grade level in the Federal service. Specialized experience for this position includes:

Editing legal or regulatory written documents written by others to ensure adherence to style and formatting requirements prior to developed for publication; AND

Recognizing and analyzing production problems and developing solutions to the problems; AND

Communicating information effectively and diplomatically to internal and/or external audiences in furtherance to program goals.

OR

EDUCATION: A master's or equivalent graduate degree or 2 full years of progressively higher level graduate education leading to such a degree or LL.B. or J.D., if related.

OR

COMBINATION OF EDUCATION AND EXPERIENCE: Note: Only graduate study in excess of the first year (18 semester hours) is qualifying for the GS-9.

NOTE: Undergraduate and Graduate Education: Must have included a total of 15 semester hours in an appropriate scientific, technical, or social science field(s), and at least one course above the introductory level in the field(s) covered by the position. For technical manuals and specifications writers or editors, the equivalent of 15 semester hours may have been gained through vocational or educational training above the high school level at a public, private, or Armed Forces school.

Additional information

We may select from this announcement or any other source to fill one or more vacancies.

This announcement may be used to fill like positions in other organizations within the National Archives and Records Administration.

This is a bargaining unit position, AFGE Council 260.

We offer opportunities for telework, per Agency policy.

We offer opportunities for alternative and flexible work schedules, per Agency policy.

Qualifications

You've got to meet these requirements by the closing date of this announcement.

Specialised Experience: For the GS-09, you must have one year of specialised experience at a level of difficulty and responsibility equivalent to the GS-07 grade level in the Federal service. Specialised experience for this position includes:

Editing legal or regulatory written documents written by other people, to make sure they stick to the style and formatting requirements before they're developed for publication; AND

Spotting and analysing production problems and coming up with fixes for them; AND

Getting information across well and diplomatically to internal and/or external audiences, to help the program goals along.

OR

EDUCATION: A master's or equivalent graduate degree or 2 full years of progressively higher level graduate education leading to such a degree or LL.B. or J.D., if related.

OR

COMBINATION OF EDUCATION AND EXPERIENCE: Note: Only graduate study past the first year (18 semester hours) counts as qualifying for the GS-9.

NOTE: Undergraduate and Graduate Education: Must have included a total of 15 semester hours in an appropriate scientific, technical, or social science field(s), and at least one course above the introductory level in the field(s) the position covers. For technical manuals and specifications writers or editors, the equivalent of 15 semester hours may have come through vocational or educational training above the high school level at a public, private, or Armed Forces school.
